extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of communication, media studies, cultural studies, journalism, and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and organizes James Carey’s evaluative principles for understanding communication, media technologies, and their effects on culture, democracy, and scholarship — emphasizing the ritual vs. transmission distinction and nation-specific inquiry. Intended for analysts applying Carey's framework to media, policy, or research design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space/time bias of communication technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication technologies promote what Innis (and Carey following him) called a 'bias' in cultures either to space or to time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify technologies as space-binding (light, portable, promoting organization and control over large territories) or time-binding (supporting permanence, limited communities, oral traditions). Examples: the printing press and electronic media are space-binding; speech, papyrus, and pre-print manuscript technologies are time-binding. Indicators include dominant symbols and language (e.g., 'voyage, discovery, movement, expansion, empire, control' for space-oriented worlds). Use portability/weight, modes of transmission, and prevailing cultural symbols to assess bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission view of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: A model that characterizes communication in terms of messages, information, and commands extended across space (transportation imagery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying or critiquing the transmission view, look for emphasis on extension of messages across geography for the purpose of control, and analysis that reduces communication to transport/flow of information. Recognize that this was dominant in empirical research Carey criticized. Beware of treating this view as the whole of communication — it must be balanced with ritual perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual (culturalist) view of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: A model that treats communication as the maintenance of society in time — the representation of shared beliefs, tradition, continuity, and attachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify practices framed as sacred ceremonies, rituals, or acts that draw people together in fellowship. Use this view to analyze how media sustain collective memory, moral perspective, and communal continuity. Carey argues scholarship should incorporate this model, not ignore it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual requirement: incorporate both ritual and transmission views
rubrics_metrics.description: A fully developed understanding of communication requires both the ritual and the transmission views; modern societies depend on both forms of communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate media, policies, or scholarship for whether they acknowledge and analyze the tension and interaction between extending messages in space and maintaining society in time. Assess societal health in terms of balance between these two functions; identify strains (e.g., expansion of space creating pressures on communal foundations) when one predominates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nation-specific empirical orientation ('useful ethnocentrism')
rubrics_metrics.description: Research should not be merely the application of abstract universal theory to general data; both theory and data should reflect the life and times of a single nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a focused, nation-bound analysis (Carey’s 'useful ethnocentrism') when studying media and culture: trace how local historical, political, and material conditions shape communication practices. For instance, analyze how printing, telegraph, railroads, radio, TV, computers, and the Internet specifically shaped American space and communal organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study effects of media on permanence and wellbeing of communal life
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarship should reference and explore the effects of communication technologies on the permanence and wellbeing of communal life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame research questions and policy analysis around how technologies alter communal continuity, memory, civic virtue, and institutions. Look for empirical interest in whether and how media practices sustain or erode democratic institutions and the 'wisdom of experience.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid technological determinism; treat technologies as cultural artifacts (homunculi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologies are products of human 'mind' and social relations and should not be viewed as strictly determining social order; they operate as 'homunculi' — concrete embodiments and templates for producing social relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing technology's social effects, emphasize that technologies carry human purposes and intelligibility and thus shape but do not deterministically cause social arrangements. Analyze both the cultural origins of a technology and the ways its intelligibility enables independent 'will' in social contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political control as mechanism to moderate technology's bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The bias of technology can be controlled only by politics — by curtailing expansionist tendencies and creating avenues for democratic discussion and participation beyond technological control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy prescriptions should not aim to eliminate technologies but to ameliorate harmful social effects and preserve space for oral/communal practices. Evaluate whether regulations and democratic forums exist or could be created to channel technological impacts toward public goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-fold analytic axis for technology's cultural effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in communication technology affect culture by (1) altering the structure of interests (the things thought about), (2) changing the character of symbols (the things thought with), and (3) changing the nature of the community (the arena in which thought developed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three dimensions as explicit lenses in empirical or theoretical studies of media: ask what new topics become salient, how symbolic resources and metaphors shift, and how community boundaries/arenas are remade by a technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture as the central portal for studying communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication should be analyzed through culture — not treated as a residual category in social analysis but as the portal through which to see and understand communication and the social order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame theoretical and empirical work so that culture (rituals, practices, symbols, institutions) is the primary object through which media effects are interpreted. Avoid reducing cultural inquiry to secondary status behind technical or purely instrumental analyses.
